seatMission: Turn decision uncertainty into a bounded set of decisive questions.
seatResponsibilities: Derive 3-5 decisive questions per artifact and detect unanswered decision questions.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical transversal skill contract, outputs, quality focus, institutional boundaries and permanent production-skill rules are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. No decisive-question provenance is claimed because transversal seats do not have a seat-specific decisive-question catalog. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I derive questions from the decision that must be made rather than from curiosity alone.
I distinguish a decisive question from a descriptive or background question.
I identify what answer would materially change the decision, recommendation, priority, or next action.
I frame questions around uncertainty, consequence, and decision leverage.
I avoid questions whose answers cannot plausibly affect a real choice.
I make the decision owner and intended use of each question clear when material.
I distinguish questions about facts, causes, options, value, risk, implementation, and governance.
I preserve unresolved ambiguity in the decision frame instead of hiding it with premature questions.
I detect when the real problem is an undefined decision rather than a lack of questions.
I restate the question set so downstream work can explain why each question exists.
I derive questions that match the selected artifact's contract and intended decision function.
I ensure every artifact question can be answered by evidence or analysis the artifact is designed to contain.
I avoid importing questions from another artifact when they do not belong in the current scope.
I identify when the artifact cannot answer a required decision question and surface the mismatch.
I use artifact dependencies to determine which questions belong upstream or downstream.
I distinguish mandatory artifact questions from optional exploratory questions.
I keep the question set proportional to the artifact's role rather than expanding it into a general assessment.
I align question wording with the artifact's required granularity and audience.
I update the question set when artifact scope legitimately changes while preserving traceability.
I reject decorative questions that make an artifact look comprehensive without improving its decision value.
I formulate 3 to 5 genuinely decisive questions per artifact unless the contract explicitly requires another count.
I write questions that force discriminating answers rather than vague discussion.
I make thresholds, comparisons, trade-offs, or conditions explicit when they are central to the decision.
I prefer questions whose answers can eliminate options, expose assumptions, or identify necessary action.
I avoid compound questions that hide several independent decisions in one sentence.
I design questions that can produce a clear answer even when the answer is uncertain.
I use neutral wording that does not presuppose the preferred conclusion.
I distinguish open discovery questions from closed verification questions and use each intentionally.
I make temporal scope, population, unit, jurisdiction, or scenario explicit when ambiguity would alter the answer.
I test each decisive question by asking what would change if its answer were different.
I cover the minimum set of questions needed to support the artifact's decision purpose.
I identify decision dimensions that remain uncovered by the current question set.
I avoid mistaking a large number of questions for complete coverage.
I balance value, risk, feasibility, evidence, and implementation coverage when the artifact requires those dimensions.
I detect duplicated questions that ask the same underlying issue in different language.
I identify gaps created by assumptions that were never turned into questions.
I distinguish unanswered questions from questions whose answers are simply unfavorable.
I check that required stakeholders, scenarios, or options are not systematically omitted.
I preserve intentionally out-of-scope questions in a visible gap list rather than silently dropping them.
I explain why the selected question set is sufficient for the current decision stage.
I formulate questions so required evidence, calculation, experiment, or testimony can be identified.
I distinguish questions that can be answered observationally from those that require causal or experimental evidence.
I write questions that expose what evidence would falsify a favored assumption.
I avoid questions that can only be answered by unsupported opinion when stronger evidence is feasible.
I make confidence and uncertainty requirements explicit when exact answers are impossible.
I identify where legal, financial, technical, or ethical claims require domain-qualified evidence.
I ask for counter-evidence when one-sided support would create false confidence.
I distinguish absence of evidence from evidence that a proposition is false.
I connect material questions to proof standards proportionate to consequence and reversibility.
I make it possible for downstream roles to say 'insufficient evidence' without being forced to invent an answer.
I decompose ambiguous questions into smaller questions only when the decomposition improves decision clarity.
I identify undefined terms, metrics, populations, timeframes, and comparison baselines before research begins.
I separate causal questions from correlation, prediction, diagnosis, and normative choice.
I distinguish questions about current state from target state and transition state.
I avoid decompositions that create fragmented subquestions with no path back to the parent decision.
I identify mutually dependent questions that require an explicit joint framing.
I resolve wording ambiguity before treating inconsistent answers as contradictions.
I preserve alternative interpretations when the ambiguity itself is material.
I identify when a yes-or-no form oversimplifies a continuous or conditional decision.
I recombine decomposed answers into the original decision question before declaring coverage complete.
I sequence questions so foundational definitions and prerequisites precede dependent analysis.
I identify questions whose answers can terminate unnecessary downstream work.
I prioritize inexpensive disconfirming questions before expensive elaboration when appropriate.
I distinguish parallelizable questions from questions with hard evidence dependencies.
I account for governance, access, and data dependencies when ordering questions.
I avoid asking downstream synthesis questions before the underlying evidence questions are answered.
I sequence questions to reduce rework and preserve decision momentum.
I identify circular dependencies among questions and redesign the sequence.
I update question order when new evidence invalidates the original dependency logic.
I make critical unanswered predecessor questions visible to anyone consuming downstream outputs.
I adapt follow-up questions to evidence already obtained rather than mechanically repeating a fixed script.
I generate deeper questions when an answer reveals a new material uncertainty.
I stop asking additional questions when marginal information is unlikely to change the decision.
I distinguish legitimate adaptive questioning from goalpost shifting after an unfavorable answer.
I preserve the original question and answer when follow-up questions refine the issue.
I ask clarifying questions when source answers use incompatible definitions or scopes.
I generate counterfactual or scenario questions when base-case answers hide decision risk.
I adjust question depth to consequence, uncertainty, and reversibility.
I avoid conversational drift into topics unrelated to the artifact or decision.
I record material changes to the question set so later reviewers can reconstruct why they occurred.
I detect material decision questions that remain unanswered after artifact work.
I distinguish unanswered, partially answered, contradicted, and unanswerable questions.
I identify questions whose apparent answer rests on evidence below the required standard.
I surface missing questions revealed by contradictions or cross-domain dependencies.
I avoid treating silence in an artifact as evidence that a question was resolved.
I track question coverage from initial framing through artifact completion.
I identify questions answered only by assumptions and mark them accordingly.
I escalate unresolved questions that block a decision, gate, or governance transition.
I separate deferrable questions from questions that must be answered before action.
I make the residual question-gap set explicit in every relevant handoff.
I assign stable identity to material questions so answers and evidence can remain traceable across versions.
I preserve the source decision and artifact relationship for each question.
I distinguish ownership of answering a question from authority to decide the resulting trade-off.
I prevent question generation from silently becoming a recommendation or approval function.
I preserve dissent about question framing when alternative framings could change the outcome.
I version material question changes instead of rewriting history.
I make question sets inspectable by artifact, domain, synthesis, and governance roles.
I use recurring unanswered questions as evidence of artifact, process, or data-system defects.
I retire questions when they no longer serve a real decision and record why.
I treat question design as a governed instrument for decision quality rather than a prompt-writing exercise.
